analysis.one_liner: Lets workers divert part of their Social Security taxes into personal investment accounts, with guaranteed benefits cut proportionally.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced September 9, 2004, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or more than one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let workers born in 1950 or later divert a slice of their Social Security payroll taxes — 10% of wages up to $10,000 (indexed) and 5% of wages above that — into personal, tax-free investment accounts run much like the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan [S2] [S3]. Balances would be invested in government-run funds, or, once the account passed a $7,000 threshold, in private investment options certified by a new board; at retirement, workers would buy a Board-approved inflation-protected annuity from private insurers [S3]. In exchange, each participant's guaranteed Social Security benefit would be reduced in proportion to the money diverted [S2] [S3]. A guarantee clause would have the Treasury pay the difference out of the Social Security trust fund if someone's annuity fell below the promised level [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Younger workers would get accounts that are their own property — inheritable if they die before retirement, exempt from income tax when drawn, and potentially growing faster than the trust fund's bonds. Asset management firms would gain a new stream of customers managing payroll contributions, and insurance companies would gain a captive annuity market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Younger workers; fund managers and insurers

how_it_helps.text: Participants divert 10% of wages up to a $10,000 base amount (indexed after 2005) and 5% of wages above it into a personal account, invested through funds structured like the federal Thrift Savings Plan with a 65/35 default stock-bond mix and options to shift allocations [S2] [S3].

Account balances are treated as the participant's property, pass to named beneficiaries or the estate on death, and qualified distributions are excluded from gross income — benefits traditional Social Security does not offer [S3].

The bill guarantees promised benefit levels: if a retiree's annuity pays less than the minimum, the Treasury supplements it from the Social Security trust fund, and a second clause tops up anyone whose combined benefit falls short of what the old formula would have paid [S3].
The bill directs the Treasury to begin reducing FICA tax rates as the program matures [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Every participant's guaranteed Social Security benefit is cut in proportion to the contributions diverted, so retirement security shifts partly onto market returns [S2] [S3]. The transition would divert Social Security trust fund surpluses into a transition fund and require issuing transition bonds, and the guarantee is backstopped by the same trust fund [S2] [S3]. Fees charged by private managers and insurers come out of account balances; the bill requires cost disclosure but sets no fee cap [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers via benefit cuts; taxpayers via transition borrowing

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed benefits are reduced for every participant by a formula tied to the amount diverted, so a worker whose investments underperform retires with less than current law provides; the government guarantee only fills a shortfall in the final annuity payment, and it draws on the Social Security trust fund [S2] [S3].

Workers are enrolled by default — anyone born in 1950 or later is a 'participating individual' unless they affirmatively file to opt out — and their traditional benefit is permanently reduced from the first diverted dollar [S3].

The transition is expensive: trust fund surpluses would be swept into a Self-Liquidating Social Security Transition Fund and transition bonds issued, adding federal borrowing during the decades when diverted payroll taxes no longer fund current retirees' benefits [S2] [S3].

Private fund companies and annuity issuers stand between workers and their savings; the bill requires annual plain-language disclosure of administrative costs but lets the market set fees, which come directly out of account earnings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real trade, not a free lunch: inheritable, tax-free accounts and a hard government guarantee in exchange for proportionally smaller guaranteed checks, exposure to market swings, transition borrowing, and a permanent new fee stream for financial firms. How any individual fares would depend heavily on investment results, and the country would carry decades of transition debt. It is a substantial redesign of the nation's largest social program, and the costs fall on the same workers it purports to help.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2004, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. John Sununu introduced the bill on September 9, 2004; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
One Senate Republican cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
No further action appears in the record — the bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor action, and it died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Supporters of Social Security as it exists kept the program unchanged. Workers who would have borne the benefit reductions and market risk kept their current guaranteed benefits; asset managers and insurers lost what would have been a very large new market.

for.name: Sen. John E. Sununu
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans were attached to the bill — the sponsor and one cosponsor — with no Democratic support, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee let it sit.

industries.industry: Asset managers and mutual fund companies
industries.note: The bill would certify private investment companies to offer 'Tier III' investment options holding workers' redirected Social Security contributions, creating a large new stream of assets under private management. The fees these firms charge come out of account balances, reducing workers' retirement savings.

Retirees would have to convert account balances into Board-approved, inflation-indexed annuities sold by Board-certified private insurers, guaranteeing insurers a captive customer base. Their pricing on those annuities determines how much retirement income workers actually receive.
